title: Interaction Modes and Team APIs

know: The three interaction modes: collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating, with the cost of each.
What a team API contains: what the team owns, how to ask it for something, what it promises, how it communicates.
believe: An interaction nobody chose becomes a queue or a standing meeting.
Collaboration is expensive and should have an end date.
can_do: Choose a mode for a pair of teams and say when it should change.
Read dependency queues and recurring meetings as signs of a wrong or unchosen mode.

audience.who: Executives (CTO, CPO, VP, Director) who must choose how two teams work together, and individual contributors who want to follow the reasoning.
already_knows: How software teams work: tickets, stand-ups, releases, APIs, on-call
Chapter 1's four levers and its definition of an interface as an agreed way for work or knowledge to cross between teams

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a described relation between two teams, the reader names the mode it is in, the mode it should be in and what would have to exist for the change.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A payments team and a fraud team have had a joint stand-up every day for fourteen months, and neither can release without the other. Which mode are they in, which should they be in, and what would have to exist first?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Open-ended collaboration; it should become X-as-a-Service (or the boundary is wrong and the teams should merge or be re-cut); it needs a defined interface or contract between the two, with an owner, and an end date for the collaboration.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter contains a filled-in team API a reader could copy.
Concepts taken from a named source name the book and the concept; rules of thumb are presented as that author's rule of thumb; anything applied beyond the source is marked as the author's extension.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

thesis.question: How should two teams work together, and how is that agreement made explicit?
thesis.claim: Two teams should work together in one of three modes — collaboration for a limited time when a boundary is still being discovered, X-as-a-Service when one can consume what the other provides without talking, and facilitating when one helps the other learn — and the choice should be written down in a team API that says what the team owns, how to ask it for something and what it promises; a mode that was never chosen shows up as a dependency queue or a meeting that never ends.
thesis.disputed_by: The belief that teams should collaborate closely by default, and that writing down how teams interact is bureaucracy that good relationships make unnecessary.
thesis.so_what: A leader reads every recurring cross-team meeting and every dependency ticket queue as a question — which mode is this, and did anyone choose it — and gives each collaboration an end date.
thesis.how_why: Collaboration costs both teams attention for as long as it lasts, which is why it is worth paying only while something is being discovered; a service costs the provider up front and the consumer almost nothing afterwards; facilitating costs the helping team time now so that the helped team needs neither afterwards. Unwritten interactions default to whatever the two managers' relationship allows and change when either of them leaves.

supporting_claims.claim: An interaction between two teams that nobody chose defaults to asking people, and it shows up as a dependency queue when one team needs the other and as a meeting that never ends when both need each other.

Three modes cover the ways two teams can work together, and they differ in who pays and when: collaboration costs both teams attention for as long as it lasts, X-as-a-Service costs the provider up front and the consumer almost nothing afterwards, and facilitating costs the helping team time now so that the helped team needs no help later.

The chosen mode is made explicit in a team API, one page that says what the team owns, how to ask it for something, what it promises and how it communicates, so that the agreement does not depend on two managers' relationship.

A mode is chosen per pair of teams and for a period, and changing it requires something to exist first: a defined interface with an owner before collaboration can become a service, and an end date before a collaboration or a facilitation starts.

Writing the interaction down does not replace cooperation: the team API states how to reach a team and what it promises, it is kept to one page, and collaboration remains the right mode while a boundary is still being discovered.

role.contribution: Turns the interface lever of chapter 1 into three concrete modes and one written artefact.

additional_patterns.applies_to: three-modes, unchosen-mode, team-api, choose-a-mode, end-date: each supplies the terms the next uses

flow.rationale: The reader meets a queue nobody decided on before any vocabulary, so the modes arrive as the answer to a question already asked. The modes come before the explanation of the default, because the default can only be named as collaboration without limits once collaboration is defined. The team API follows the explanation, because the reason for writing the choice down is that unwritten choices do not last. The two patterns come after the page because both end by writing a line into it; choosing first and writing afterwards would give the procedure a last step whose object the reader has not seen. Misuses and the disagreement between sources follow the patterns they qualify. The worked example comes after all of them so that it can use every term, and the AI section is a coda that tests the written page against a new kind of reader. Putting the team API first would present a template with no reason to fill it in.

hook.content: Corvane's platform team of five was created in 2022 to help the product teams release faster. By 2024 every launch of eleven product teams waited on it, and nobody had ever decided how a product team was supposed to use it.

bridge.from_reader_world: Most readers know a team that everyone waits on, or a weekly cross-team meeting that nobody remembers starting and nobody dares to cancel.
bridge.to_topic: Both are what an interaction between two teams looks like when nobody chose how the two should work together.

thesis_statement.text: Two teams should work together in one of three modes, collaboration for a limited time, X-as-a-Service or facilitating, and the choice should be written down in a team API; a mode nobody chose shows up as a dependency queue or a meeting that never ends.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See a helping team become a queue because nobody defined what it offered.
Learn the three interaction modes and what each costs.
Understand why an unchosen mode turns into a queue or a standing meeting.
Write the agreement down as a one-page team API, with a filled-in example to copy.
Choose a mode for a pair of teams and give every collaboration an end date and an exit.
Recognize the common misuses of the modes.
Know where the sources disagree about writing interactions down.
Follow Corvane's platform team as it changes mode.
See what AI changes about interactions between teams.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's platform team was created to help product teams release faster and became the place every launch waited, because nobody had decided how a product team should use it.

evidence.what: Stage 3 in the ledger: a platform team of five formed in 2022; eleven product teams from 2023; in 2024, at 180 people, 14 open launch requests and a median lead time of 19 days, up from 4.
evidence.shows: A team meant to help became a queue without anyone deciding that it should.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two teams should work in one of three modes, written down in a team API, and a mode nobody chose shows up as a queue or a meeting that never ends; the chapter goes from the case to the modes, the default, the team API, two patterns, the misuses, the disagreement, the worked example and AI.

transition_in.carries_over: A helping team that became a queue, and the reader's own versions of it.
transition_in.introduces: The claim that the mode was never chosen, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: A Service Nobody Defined
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane's platform team became a queue because what it offered, how to ask for it and what it promised were never stated, so every launch was a ticket worked through jointly with a platform engineer.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case of an unchosen interaction and its cost, which the rest of the chapter names and repairs.

flow.rationale: The reader needs what the team was for, what was left undecided and what followed, in that order, to see that the queue was a default and not a decision.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's short account of the platform team that became a queue.
transition_in.introduces: The case in full: how a launch worked and what had never been decided.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2023 and 2024 a product team at Corvane, the fictional company this book follows, released a change by filing a launch request and waiting for one of five platform engineers to check and release it by hand.

evidence.what: The platform team, led by Lena Brandt, held the deployment scripts from 2023; a launch was a hand check of migrations, configuration and the way back, then a release in a slot; all eleven product teams needed it for some launches and three for every launch.
evidence.shows: Sets out the interaction as it worked in practice.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three things had never been decided: what the platform team offered, how a product team should ask for it, and what the platform team promised in return.

transition_in.carries_over: How a launch worked in practice.
transition_in.introduces: What nobody had decided about it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With nothing decided, the default was to ask a person, so each launch became joint work between a platform engineer and a product team, and five engineers doing joint work with eleven teams produced a queue.

evidence.what: 14 open launch requests at the peak in 2024; of 19 days of median lead time about 17 were waiting for a launch slot.
evidence.shows: The cost of the default, in waiting.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: Three undecided things.
transition_in.introduces: What filled the gap, and what it cost.

sections.heading: Three Interaction Modes and What Each Costs
sections.controlling_idea: Two teams can work together in three modes, collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating, and the modes differ in who pays and for how long.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the three modes and the cost of each, which is the first half of the thesis.

flow.rationale: The definition of a mode comes first, then the three side by side, then one paragraph per row of the table in the table's order: the two modes that get work done, contrasted by who pays, and then the mode that moves a skill. Choosing between modes before each one's cost is explained would be choosing by name.

transition_in.carries_over: A joint way of working that nobody chose.
transition_in.introduces: The small set of ways two teams can choose to work together.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An interaction mode is the way two teams have agreed to work together for the time being, and Team Topologies names three, which apply between the four team types of the previous chapter.

evidence.what: Skelton and Pais's three core interaction modes: collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating; their note that not all communication and collaboration is good and that team interfaces should set expectations.
evidence.shows: The modes are a named source's concept, and the source's reason for having them is to limit communication to what the work needs.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three modes differ in what the two teams do, who pays, when the mode is right and when it should end.

evidence.what: Mode | What the two teams do | Who pays, and when | Right when | Ends when. Rows: collaboration, X-as-a-Service, facilitating.
evidence.shows: The modes can be told apart by their cost and their end condition.

transition_in.carries_over: Three named modes.
transition_in.introduces: The three side by side.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Collaboration, two teams working on one problem as if they were one team, is the fastest way to discover something and costs both teams attention for as long as it lasts, so it is worth paying only while a boundary or an interface is still unknown.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "Collaboration is good for rapid discovery and avoiding hand-offs and delays, but the downside is a higher level of cognitive load." The authors' rule of thumb, in the author's checklist: collaborate with at most one other team at a time.
evidence.shows: The source itself treats collaboration as a cost to be limited, and gives the limit as a rule of thumb.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

transition_in.carries_over: The table's first row.
transition_in.introduces: Why collaboration is expensive and when it is worth it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In X-as-a-Service one team provides something another team uses without talking to it, which costs the provider work up front and the consumer almost nothing afterwards, and works only if the service is defined well enough to be used without help.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "The X-as-a-Service model works well only if the service boundary is well chosen and well implemented, with a good service-management practice from the team providing the service."
evidence.shows: The condition under which the cheapest mode for the consumer is available at all.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

transition_in.carries_over: A mode both teams pay for continuously.
transition_in.introduces: A mode one team pays for once.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In facilitating one team helps another learn to do something itself, which costs the helping team time now and is finished when the helped team no longer needs the help.

evidence.what: Team Topologies' facilitating mode, as distilled in the author's checklist: the goal is the helped team's self-sufficiency, the helper does not take over the helped team's work, and both understand the help is temporary.
evidence.shows: Facilitating has an end by definition, which separates it from a permanent dependency.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); the author's record team-interaction-modes

transition_in.carries_over: Two modes for getting work done.
transition_in.introduces: The mode for moving a skill.

sections.heading: Why an Unchosen Mode Becomes a Queue or a Standing Meeting
sections.controlling_idea: When nobody chooses a mode, the two teams fall into collaboration without its limits, which appears as a queue when one team needs the other and as a recurring meeting when both need each other.

advances_thesis.how: Explains the mechanism behind the opening case and gives the reader the two symptoms to read.

flow.rationale: The claim about the default comes first, then the symptoms that let a reader test it, then the case that limits the symptoms, placed directly after them so that the reader does not conclude every meeting is a fault. The reason unwritten agreements do not last comes last because it is the reason for the next section; placed earlier it would separate the limiting case from the symptoms it limits.

transition_in.carries_over: Three modes, each with a cost and an end.
transition_in.introduces: What happens when none of them is chosen.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When no mode is chosen, people ask each other, and asking is collaboration without an end date or a limit on the number of teams; it queues when the need runs one way and becomes a standing meeting when it runs both ways.
A dependency queue, a recurring cross-team meeting, a service that needs constant help and a helper who never leaves each point to a mode in practice that differs from the mode the work needs.

evidence.what: What you see | Mode in practice | Mode the work probably needs | What is missing. Four rows: ticket queue at one team; recurring meeting of two teams that cannot release alone; consumers who keep asking for help with a service; a helping team still doing the work after a year.
evidence.shows: Each symptom can be read as a mode and a missing thing.

transition_in.carries_over: The two default shapes.
transition_in.introduces: Four symptoms, each read as a mode.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A recurring meeting is not a symptom when it has an owner, a purpose and an output, as Corvane's weekly rules session of 2022 had.

evidence.what: The 2022 fix: rule changes published as a versioned schema and reviewed in a weekly rules session owned by Core, with Priya Nambiar deciding and the decisions recorded.
evidence.shows: A standing meeting can be a chosen team interface; the test is owner, purpose and output.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: Meetings and queues read as symptoms.
transition_in.introduces: A recurring meeting that is a designed interface, and the test that tells the two apart.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An unwritten way of working lasts only as long as the relationship between the two people who hold it, and changes when either of them leaves.

evidence.what: Chapter 1's two engineers who talk every Thursday: an interface agreed between two people leaves the company with either of them; the same holds for two managers who have an understanding.
evidence.shows: Why choosing a mode is not enough unless it is written where others can read it.

transition_in.carries_over: A meeting that lasted because it had an owner and a written output.
transition_in.introduces: Why a chosen mode that is only spoken does not last.

sections.heading: The Team API: The Agreement Written Down
sections.controlling_idea: A team API is one page that says what a team owns, how to ask it for something, what it promises and how it communicates, and it is what makes a chosen mode readable by people who were not in the room.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the written artefact of the thesis and the filled-in example the reader can copy.

flow.rationale: The definition and its parts lead straight to the example, and the example comes before the comment on it, so that the reader can check the example against the parts and is not told what to think of it before seeing it. The comparison with the team charter comes last: between the parts and the example it would interrupt them, and it is only useful to a reader who already knows what a team API holds.

transition_in.carries_over: Agreements that live in two people's heads.
transition_in.introduces: The page that holds them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team API, Team Topologies' term, is the written description of how to work with a team; it describes the team's team interfaces in chapter 3's sense and lists its software interfaces as one item among several.

evidence.what: Team Topologies' team API, as distilled in the author's record team-first-thinking: code and endpoints, versioning, documentation, working practices and communication channels, priorities and roadmap.
evidence.shows: The artefact and its contents come from a named source.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); the author's record team-first-thinking

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The contents of a team API reduce to four questions, to which this book adds a fifth part: the team's current interactions, each with its mode and end date.

evidence.what: Part | The question it answers | What goes in it. Rows: what we own; how to ask us; what we promise; how we communicate; current interactions (the author's addition).
evidence.shows: The reader can see what a complete team API holds and which part is the author's extension.

transition_in.carries_over: The source's list of contents.
transition_in.introduces: The same contents as four questions and one addition.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's platform team wrote its team API at the end of the 2024 pilot, the quarter in which it rebuilt its release path so that a product team could run it, and the page fits on one sheet.

evidence.what: The filled-in team API of Corvane's platform team: what we own (the release path, the deployment scripts, the shared infrastructure and the shared data model), what we do not do, how to ask us, what we promise (including alerts answered at any hour by the platform engineer on call), how we communicate, current interactions with modes and end dates.
evidence.shows: A complete example a reader could copy and edit.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: The five parts in the abstract.
transition_in.introduces: One team's page, filled in.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four things make that page usable as a pattern: it says what the team does not do, its promises carry numbers, each interaction has a mode and an end date, and it has a named user and a measure.

evidence.what: User: an engineer in a product team who has never spoken to the platform team. Outcome measure: the share of that team's needs met without a person on the platform team being involved, and whether a consumer can say what the team promises.
evidence.shows: States the pattern's user and outcome measure, as the book requires of every pattern.

transition_in.carries_over: The filled-in page.
transition_in.introduces: What to notice in it before copying it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team API is the outward-facing part of a team charter: the charter of Scaling People also says why the team exists and what it is measured on, and its sections on provided and dependent interfaces are the part other teams read.

evidence.what: The eight-section team charter from the Scaling People workbooks (mission, vision, customers, metrics, strategic importance, risks, provided interfaces, dependent interfaces), as described in the author's record team-charter.
evidence.shows: Where the team API sits relative to a document many organizations already have.
evidence.source: Claire Hughes Johnson, Scaling People (2023); the author's record team-charter

transition_in.carries_over: A team API and what makes it usable.
transition_in.introduces: The neighbouring document many organizations already have, and how the two relate.

sections.heading: Pattern: Choose a Mode for Each Pair of Teams
sections.controlling_idea: The mode is chosen for one pair of teams at a time, by asking whether something between them is still unknown, whether one can use what the other provides without talking, and whether one lacks a skill the other has.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the modes into a procedure a leader can run on a pair of teams.

flow.rationale: The procedure with its user and measure comes first, then its second step as a figure, then the defaults that team types supply. The defaults come last because they shorten a procedure the reader must first have seen whole; given first, they would read as a rule that replaces the three questions.

transition_in.carries_over: A page that records a mode.
transition_in.introduces: How the mode on it is chosen.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Choosing a mode is a short procedure for the leads of two teams and the manager they share, and it worked when both teams give the same answer to which mode they are in and until when.

evidence.what: Steps: name the pair and what crosses between them; ask the three questions in order; write the mode and its end date into both team APIs; set the date on which it is read again. User: the two team leads and their shared manager. Outcome measure: both teams name the same mode and end date; no team is in collaboration with more than one other team; the wait at the dependency falls.
evidence.shows: A reader can run the choice and tell whether it worked.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three questions are asked in a fixed order, and each answer leads to one mode or to the next question.

evidence.what: Mermaid decision flow: is something between the two teams still unknown (collaboration, with an end date); can one team use what the other provides without talking to it (X-as-a-Service); does one lack a skill the other can teach (facilitating); otherwise the two teams need no interaction.
evidence.shows: The choice as a flow, including the outcome that two teams need no standing interaction at all.

transition_in.carries_over: The procedure's second step.
transition_in.introduces: The three questions drawn as a flow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The team types of the previous chapter supply a default mode for most pairs, and a pair whose mode contradicts its types is a signal that a team is misdescribed.

evidence.what: Team Topologies' typical pairings, as distilled in the author's record team-interaction-modes: platform and complicated-subsystem teams mostly provide a service, enabling teams mostly facilitate, stream-aligned teams collaborate only for discovery.
evidence.shows: The defaults come from the source and shorten the procedure.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); the author's record team-interaction-modes

transition_in.carries_over: A choice made from three questions.
transition_in.introduces: The defaults that team types give.

sections.heading: Pattern: Give Every Collaboration an End Date and an Exit
sections.controlling_idea: A collaboration starts with an end date, and at that date it leaves by one of three exits: a service with a defined interface and an owner, a changed boundary, or one renewal with a stated reason.

advances_thesis.how: States what has to exist for a mode to change, which is the part of the thesis a leader acts on.

flow.rationale: The rule comes before the exits because the exits are what the end date forces the two teams to choose between; exits without a date would describe a decision nobody is made to take.

transition_in.carries_over: Collaboration as one outcome of the choice.
transition_in.introduces: The rule that keeps collaboration from becoming permanent.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every collaboration, and every facilitation, gets an end date on the day it starts, for the two teams' leads, and the measure is the number of collaborations past their date.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "Collaborate on potentially ambiguous interfaces until the interfaces are proven stable and functional." The time box in weeks is the author's recommendation, not the source's.
evidence.shows: The source gives the end condition; the date is the author's way of making someone check it.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the end date a collaboration leaves by one of three exits: it becomes a service if a defined interface with an owner exists that the consumer can use without talking; if no interface can be drawn, the boundary is wrong and the teams are merged or re-cut; and if the unknown is still unknown for a stated reason, it is renewed once.

evidence.what: Three exits: a service (needs a defined interface, an owner, and a consumer who can use it without help); a boundary change (merge the teams or move what both keep changing to one of them, chapter 4's subject); one renewal with a new date and a written reason.
evidence.shows: Names what would have to exist for the change of mode, which is what the reader is asked to do with a described pair of teams.

transition_in.carries_over: An end date.
transition_in.introduces: What is decided when it arrives.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: Collaboration Everywhere, the Service That Is Not One, the Page Nobody Reads
sections.controlling_idea: The modes fail in three recognizable ways: collaboration as the default for every pair, a service or a facilitation in name only, and a team API written as a wall or left to go stale.

advances_thesis.how: Shows how each part of the thesis is misused, in the book's failure-pattern names.

flow.rationale: One paragraph per misuse, in the order in which the chapter introduced what is misused: collaboration, then the two modes that are faked, then the page. The page's misuse comes last because it is the objection the next section answers.

transition_in.carries_over: What to do.
transition_in.introduces: How it goes wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Collaboration as the default for every pair of teams spreads each team's attention over all its neighbours and hides what a platform or a boundary fails to provide.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "Unnecessary collaboration is particularly expensive, especially as it can mask or hide deficiencies in underlying platforms or capabilities."
evidence.shows: The source names both the cost and what it conceals; in this book's terms the result is The Overloaded Team.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A service whose consumers must ask for help each time is a queue with a service's name, and a facilitating team that does the work is a permanent dependency.

evidence.what: Corvane's Launch Queue of 2024, which the failure-patterns page files under The Review Bottleneck.
evidence.shows: The book's own case of a service in name only.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: One mode overused.
transition_in.introduces: The other two modes faked.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team API fails when it is written as a list of refusals, or written once and left, because then a crossing between teams again has no owner.

transition_in.carries_over: Misused modes.
transition_in.introduces: A misused page.

sections.heading: Where the Sources Disagree: Written Contracts or Cooperation
sections.controlling_idea: Team Topologies wants interactions limited and defined, Six Simple Rules warns that too much clarity lets people comply with their box, and the book's resolution is to write down the way in to a team and keep it to one page.

advances_thesis.how: Answers the objection that writing interactions down is bureaucracy, and states the conditions under which it is.

flow.rationale: The two positions first, then the resolution with its conditions; the reader needs both positions to judge the resolution.

transition_in.carries_over: A page that can become a wall.
transition_in.introduces: A source that says such pages usually do.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Team Topologies holds that communication between teams should be limited and defined, while Morieux and Tollman advise leaders to resist clarifying roles and processes because clarity past a threshold produces compliance in place of cooperation.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "What we need is focused communication between specific teams." Six Simple Rules: "Resist the pressure to clarify roles, decision rights, and processes."
evidence.shows: Two of the book's sources give opposite advice on the subject of this chapter.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); Yves Morieux and Peter Tollman, Six Simple Rules (2014)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Both are right about different things, and a team API respects both when it describes how to reach the team and what it promises, says nothing about what its members may refuse to care about, and is skipped where everyone still knows whom to ask.

evidence.what: Choice | What you gain | What you lose | Fits when. Rows: unwritten, by relationship; a one-page team API; a detailed service contract.
evidence.shows: The amount of writing is a trade-off with conditions, not a rule.

transition_in.carries_over: Two opposed pieces of advice.
transition_in.introduces: The resolution and when each amount of writing fits.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Corvane's Platform Team Changes Mode
sections.controlling_idea: Between 2023 and 2025 the same five platform engineers went from ticket-driven collaboration with eleven teams to a service, by way of six weeks inside one team, and a second pair of Corvane teams left an unchosen collaboration by the boundary exit.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the modes, the end date and the exits to the opening case, with the ledger's numbers.

flow.rationale: The periods in order, then what the sequence shows and what it cost, then the second case. The second case comes last because it uses the exit the first did not; before the first it would show a boundary change to a reader who has not yet seen a change of mode without one.

transition_in.carries_over: The modes, the page and the disagreement about it.
transition_in.introduces: The opening case read with them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read by period, the relation between Corvane's platform team and its product teams passed through three modes, and only the first was unchosen.

evidence.what: Period | Mode in practice | Chosen? | What existed | Result. Rows: 2023 to 2024 launch requests; pilot weeks 1 to 2 with Scheduling; pilot weeks 3 to 6; from week 7; the following two quarters.
evidence.shows: The sequence of modes with the ledger's lead times: 19 days, 6 for Scheduling, 8 and then under 7 company-wide.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: Coding agents can use what is written and cannot use what lives in a relationship, so a written team API matters more with them, and an interaction that passes through people may degrade faster as changes become cheaper to produce.

advances_thesis.how: Tests the written artefact against agents doing part of the work, with labeled claims.

flow.rationale: The observed claim first and the speculative one second, so that the reader meets the better-supported claim before the less supported one and does not weigh them equally.

transition_in.carries_over: Corvane's teams in 2024, without agents.
transition_in.introduces: The same modes when agents do part of the work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: As of November 2026, teams that use coding agents write down for the agent what a colleague would have asked in person, which makes the written part of an interaction the only part an agent can use.

evidence.what: Emerging, the author's observation and not a measured result: repositories carry instruction files that tell an agent how to build, test and follow the team's conventions; an agent reads them and has no hallway to ask in.
evidence.shows: A written team API serves a reader that cannot use a relationship; an unwritten one does not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: If agents make changes cheaper to produce, requests reach provider teams faster, and an interaction handled by people falls behind sooner than a self-service one.

evidence.what: Speculative. Illustration: Corvane's Review Wall of 2027 to 2028, merged changes per week up 2.4 times while review capacity stayed flat, median review wait from 5 hours to 31. Would be confirmed where queues at provider teams grow in step with consumers' change volume and self-service interfaces do not.
evidence.shows: Shows the reasoning on the ledger's numbers and says what would confirm it.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: A mode and a team API are the same decision at two moments: the mode is what two teams agree, and the team API is what remains of the agreement when the people who made it are not there. A queue or a standing meeting is what remains when nothing was agreed.
conclusion.so_what: A leader reads every recurring cross-team meeting and every dependency queue as a question, which mode is this and did anyone choose it, and gives each collaboration an end date.

callback.to: The platform team of five on which every launch waited.
callback.how: The reader can now say what was missing in 2023: not people, but a defined service, a way to ask and a promise, which is one page.

takeaway.content: List your team's interactions, name the mode of each, give each collaboration an end date and write one page that says how to work with your team. The checklist gives the steps.
